title: Teach the import mapper to build records

blocks.text: The nightly import reads rows from partner files, each row a map from column name to value, and turns every row into an object with `RowMapper.map`. The mapper was written for beans. The team has since turned `Shipment`, `Sensor` and the other imported types into records, and now every import fails before the first row is stored.

Finish `toRecord(...)` in `src/main/java/practice/RowMapper.java`, so that `map` builds records as well as beans. Each column is named after a component of the record, but partners send the columns in whatever order their files have, and the import adds bookkeeping columns of its own (their names start with `_`). A row that a record refuses must still be refused, with the record's own exception somewhere in what `map` throws. About ten lines.
The tests use records of their own, with components of several types.

cases.says: a row whose columns match the record's components builds an equal record, for records of different shapes
a row with a value the record's own constructor refuses is refused with that constructor's exception
a row whose columns come in another order than the record's header still puts each value in the component of its name
columns the record has no component for are left out instead of breaking the import

origin.section: A Framework That Builds an Object Empty, Then Fills It, Can't Build a Record

concepts: A record is built from outside through its canonical constructor, whose parameters getRecordComponents() lists by name and type in header order, so the record's checks run.
